entities.name: Richard de Beauchamp, 13th Earl of Warwick
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard de Beauchamp, 13th Earl of Warwick, born in 1382, emerged as a preeminent English nobleman, military commander, and diplomat during the turbulent reigns of Henry IV, Henry V, and Henry VI. A central figure in the Hundred Years' War, his career spanned over four decades, marked by distinguished service to the Lancastrian dynasty and a reputation for chivalry and martial prowess that resonated across late medieval Europe. He inherited vast estates and the earldom of Warwick in 1401, positioning him at the apex of English aristocracy and making him an indispensable asset to the Crown in both domestic and continental affairs.

Beauchamp's early career saw him fighting at the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403 against Henry Percy, and later participating in campaigns against the Welsh rebel Owain Glyndŵr. His strategic acumen was further demonstrated as Governor of Calais from 1415 to 1419, a vital English stronghold in France. He played a pivotal role in the diplomatic negotiations leading to the Treaty of Troyes in 1420, which temporarily united the crowns of England and France under Henry V. Following Henry V's premature death, Beauchamp was entrusted with the crucial responsibility of tutoring the young Henry VI, shaping the future monarch's education and moral compass. His final major appointment was as Lieutenant of Normandy and France from 1437 until his death in Rouen in 1439.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard de Beauchamp was a highly influential figure in English and French politics during the Hundred Years' War, serving three English kings and playing a key role in major diplomatic and military events like the Treaty of Troyes. His career epitomized the power and responsibility of late medieval English magnates, impacting both royal policy and the cultural ideals of chivalry.
